name: Humour effect
statement: Humorous material is recalled better than a matched non-humorous version of the same material, and manipulating humour has produced the gain only within subjects.
meaning: The test compares two or three versions of one item. Schmidt wrote sentences in humorous and non-humorous forms. Schmidt and Williams used cartoons in three forms: the original Gary Larson drawing, a literal version with the incongruous element removed, and a weird version built by pasting in an incongruity that cannot be resolved. Participants rate each item for humour, work through arithmetic, then recall without cues. What improves is access to the item rather than memory for its wording. Humour raised recall of the cartoon picture and of the gist of the caption, and left untouched the proportion of words recovered from a caption already recalled. Design decides the outcome as much as material does. Manipulated humour has produced the effect when both versions reach the same participant and not when different groups see different versions, while a participant's own humour ratings predict recall in either arrangement.

origin.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
origin.note: Six experiments comparing humorous and non-humorous versions of sentences. The paper is paywalled and its abstract was read at OpenAlex. That abstract records the effect on free recall and on cued recall, its survival when participants were warned a humorous sentence was coming, its attenuation under incidental learning, and its limitation to within-subjects manipulations. Schmidt and Williams describe the earlier literature as anecdotal or quasi-experimental, naming Kaplan and Pascoe on humorous lecture examples and two studies of humour in advertising.

evidence: Schmidt and Williams tested 84 students on 24 cartoons under a cover story about humour and mathematics, with the memory test unexpected. A pilot group of 24 rated the originals at 5.10 for humour against 3.08 for the literal versions and 3.25 for the weird ones, and rated the weird cartoons as more bizarre than the originals, 4.27 against 3.92. In the mixed list, originals were recalled at .45 for the picture, .16 for words and .40 for the caption scored leniently, against .35, .12 and .29 for literal cartoons and .37, .13 and .31 for weird ones. Literal and weird cartoons never differed. Words recovered per recalled caption ran .38, .40 and .40, with no effect of cartoon type. Originals also came out earlier in the recall protocol, at output percentile 52.89 against 58.25 and 63.24. Their second experiment gave 128 students lists holding only two of the three cartoon types. Originals beat both comparisons in every list they appeared in, and weird cartoons never beat literal ones, which is the opposite of what an incongruity or distinctiveness account predicts. They then sorted the same data by each participant's own humour rating. Cartoons in the upper half beat those in the lower half on picture recall, F(1,122) = 10.15, word recall, F(1,122) = 8.99, and caption recall scored both ways. That held inside the weird and literal lists, where the experimenters had manipulated no humour at all. Summerfelt, Lippman and Hyman report four experiments on knock-knock jokes presented with the pun intact or removed. The pun improved recall and recognition after incidental encoding. They attribute the gain to the constraint a pun places on the closing line rather than to humour itself. Carlson had participants rate stimuli for humour or for inspirational quality and reports that humour ratings predicted recall with semantic elaboration and incongruity resolution controlled. Chambers and Payne tested memory for 27 cartoons across 12 hours and found the advantage intact, and larger when the interval held sleep.

replication.headline: Schmidt and Williams obtained the effect in two experiments with new materials, recalling humorous cartoons at .45 against .35 for literal versions of the same drawings, and independent groups have since obtained it with jokes, photographs and delayed tests.
replication.detail: The 2001 experiments were built to separate humour from incongruity rather than to ask whether the effect exists, which makes them a clean check. Both produced it, and both produced it under incidental instructions, which the 1994 paper had not. Schmidt and Williams call that earlier null a Type II error. Independent work has followed. Summerfelt, Lippman and Hyman obtained better recall and recognition for jokes retaining their pun. Chambers and Payne obtained the advantage across a 12-hour delay. Noël and Picard ran two studies on younger and older adults and report the usual advantage for humorous photograph sequences in younger adults in both, with the effect surviving when incongruous sequences were added as a third comparison. The boundary sits at the design. Schmidt's 2002 abstract reports that original cartoons beat literal and weird ones within subjects, and that good recall of the humorous cartoons came at the cost of the non-humorous ones. Neither the memory effect nor the accompanying heart-rate deceleration appeared in between-subjects comparisons. The 1994 abstract states the same limitation for sentences. Rated humour is the exception: it predicted recall in both designs there, and inside lists carrying no humour manipulation in 2001.

study.cite: Schmidt, S. R., & Williams, A. R. (2001). Memory for humorous cartoons. Memory & Cognition, 29(2), 305-311.

limits: No meta-analysis of humour and memory was located. PubMed returns nothing for humour, memory and meta-analysis together, a Crossref bibliographic query on the same terms returned unrelated work, and general web search produced single studies, theses and reviews of classroom humour. Most of the literature was reachable only as abstracts. Schmidt's 1994 and 2002 papers, Summerfelt and colleagues, Carlson, Strick and colleagues, and Noël and Picard are all paywalled, so no effect size from any of them is quoted here and none is placed in the structured fields. The full text read for this entry is Schmidt and Williams, and every proportion above comes from it. Age is a hard boundary. Noël and Picard tested 19 younger and 20 older adults, then 37 and 38. They report no benefit of humour in older adults and a cost in cued recall, which disappeared once incongruity was controlled. Their explanation is an associative memory deficit meeting the incongruity that humorous material carries. The classroom case is weaker than the laboratory one. Bender, Renkl and Endres ran two between-subjects studies, 115 adults and 151 school pupils, on a narrated slideshow carrying relevant humour, irrelevant humour, relevant non-humorous examples or nothing. Relevant humour did not beat the plain control on recall in either study, with mean differences of 4.24 and 4.57 percentage points, p = .335 and p = .170, and Bayes factors of 2.74 and 2.29 favouring the null. Irrelevant humour scored below the control on transfer in the first study, mean difference 8.63 percentage points, p = .018. Vella-Brodrick, Jory and Whelan, cited by Schmidt and Williams for the finding that the effect survives experimenter-paced presentation, is an unpublished manuscript and was not read.
misreadings: Distinctiveness is not the mechanism, and this is where the effect parts company with its neighbours. Schmidt and Williams's weird cartoons were rated more bizarre than the originals and recalled no better than the literal ones, in a list where they were the odd items. An account resting on standing out predicts the reverse. Schmidt and Williams place bizarreness and orthographic distinctiveness among effects obtained in lists split half and half, and that is the company the humour effect is usually kept in. Its own dependence on a mixed list looks different once the weird cartoons are taken into account. Attention paid to the funny item is taken from its neighbours, which is a claim about competition rather than contrast. Schmidt reports that good recall of humorous material comes at the expense of non-humorous material studied nearby. Strick and colleagues tracked eye movements over texts paired with unfamiliar consumer brands. Humorous texts held gaze longer than positive or neutral ones, and that extra attention correlated with worse recognition of the brand beside them. The tests they survive differ as well. Schmidt's 1994 abstract reports humour helping free recall and cued recall alike, and Summerfelt and colleagues report it helping recall and recognition. Schmidt and Williams go further and argue that bizarreness research may be confounded, since bizarre materials are often funny, and that the humour effect appeared in their data where an effect of bizarreness did not. Surprise and incongruity are also not the mechanism. Incongruity that cannot be resolved bought nothing, and rated humour predicted recall even among cartoons the experimenters had built to carry no humour at all. Humour buys the gist and not the words. Schmidt and Williams found no effect on the proportion of words recovered from a caption already recalled, and offer that as the reason a joke is hard to retell: the point survives and the wording does not.
